object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer as represented in the billing system; everything hangs off the account number.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product/plan.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.
Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: One of the fixed set of products the company sells (e.g. CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT).

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: Price Plan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact: what a customer pays and how often, generating invoice lines.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: Feature Bundle
object_types.definition: The feature bundle a customer gets: seats, API access, SSO, etc. -- what appears on the pricing page.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: Plan Change
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, capturing who requested it, when, and its effective date.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: Start Date
object_types.definition: The date a subscription begins; always present.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: End Date
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends; optional, present only for fixed-term or cancelled subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front

object_types.name: Billing Period
object_types.definition: How often a subscription is billed.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.
Only those two. There was a quarterly once, for one customer, and it caused so much trouble that we bought them out of it.
Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: Effective Date
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: MRR
object_types.definition: Monthly recurring revenue; a derived figure normalising the plan price to a monthly amount, not stored in the source system.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. Monthly recurring revenue. It's the number I live in.
It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83.

object_types.name: Paused Flag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean indicating a subscription is paused; not part of the status enumeration but behaves similarly, causing confusion.

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused. ... Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

objectified_fact_types.description: A plan change is treated as a first-class entity (with its own change ID) rather than merely a log entry, because who made it, when it takes effect, and the new plan all need to be tracked as facts about that change.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history.

ambiguities.description: The word 'plan' is used for at least three distinct concepts: Priya's billing artefact (Price Plan), Tom's feature bundle (Feature Bundle), and sales' negotiated deal (a third, unmodeled concept). The transcript explicitly flags this terminology collision as unresolved.

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.
Only that we still call three different things "plan" and this document won't fix that. ... It won't. But it'll at least name them separately, which is a start.

ambiguities.description: It is unclear whether 'Paused' should be modeled as a fifth subscription status or as an orthogonal boolean flag; the team acknowledges it behaves like a status but is implemented as a separate boolean, causing bugs (e.g., paused subscriptions appearing in 'active' queries). This is a known inconsistency, not a clean rule.

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused. ... Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: The commercial/business rule for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run to term, prorated refund, or credit) is explicitly undecided and parked; only the current system behavior (no refund, access runs to paid-through date) is captured. Four manual credits were issued outside the system as goodwill, raising the question of whether this is now a de facto policy.

source_references.excerpt: Mid-term cancellation on annual plans. ... Then I'm parking it explicitly. What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: There is a discrepancy about whether Subscription has a single 'current price plan' field versus the plan being purely derived from plan-change history. Sam initially claims it's purely derived, then Priya reveals there's a denormalised 'current plan' field maintained by the change process, and Sam withdraws his correction. It's unclear if this denormalised field is authoritative or merely a cache that can go stale ('the change history wins and the current plan is the bug').

source_references.excerpt: One correction. You said a subscription belongs to one price plan. It doesn't, really -- that's what the plan changes are for. ... No, Sam, it does have a current plan field... And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: When an account closes and the same company returns, they are given a new account number and treated as a new customer for reporting purposes, deliberately losing historical linkage. This is a stated business rule but Tom disputes its wisdom from a product perspective, suggesting potential future change or disagreement about whether 'Account' truly represents 'Customer' over time.

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. ... Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: The number of products is described as 'fixed at three' but with a fourth already in discovery, and it's unclear whether/when this constraint (exactly CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) will change, making the value_constraint on Product potentially unstable.

source_references.excerpt: Fixed at three? ... Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: It's unclear whether the external uniqueness/frequency constraint of 'one active subscription per account per product' applies only to subscriptions in 'active' status specifically, or more broadly to any non-terminal/current subscription state (e.g., does it also block two 'trialing' subscriptions for the same product?). The transcript only discusses 'active' explicitly.

source_references.excerpt: So it's one active subscription per account per product. ... No. The system blocks it.
